forces: Orchestra with piano, celesta and two harps
performers: Orchestre de la Suisse Romande; Ernest Ansermet
intro: The third tableau of Stravinsky’s Petrushka, heard here in the original 1911 version, takes place in the Moor’s room. The Ballerina courts Petrushka’s rival to a cornet solo and a pair of borrowed waltzes, and her partner dances in two while she dances in three.

sections.label: A · Offstage drums and Feroce chords
sections.mNote: Offstage drums lead to Feroce chords in strings and wind.

sections.label: B · Bassoons, clarinet and bass clarinet
sections.mNote: Low bassoons lead into clarinet and bass clarinet in octaves

sections.label: C · Cornet and military drum
sections.mNote: The Ballerina performs her short solo.

sections.label: D · Lanner waltzes against duple metre
sections.mNote: Lanner’s waltz tunes are combined with a partner’s dance in two.

sections.label: E · Petrushka’s entrance, muted brass
sections.mNote: Muted brass play Petrushka’s cry in the Moor’s room.

cues.title: Offstage drums, rehearsals 62–63
cues.text: Offstage drums separate the scenes. Wind chords and plucked strings enter, marked Feroce stringendo (fierce and pressing forward). The bowed strings then begin heavy, swooping figures.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe full score, plate R.M.V. 127, p. 78, rehearsals 62–63; offstage drums, Feroce stringendo and Meno mosso, Pesante. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sostenuto, clarinet and bass clarinet
cues.text: The tempo slows to Sostenuto. Bassoons and tuba play low in the orchestra, and plucked strings and percussion set a steady beat. Clarinet and bass clarinet play the main tune, doubled an octave apart.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, pp. 79–80, rehearsals 64–65. The note describes the preparation and ensuing dance. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Scenery of the third tableau
cues.text: Benois gave this puppet a low sofa, a magnificent robe and paper walls painted with palms and exotic fruit. He plays with a coconut.
cues.evidence: The third tableau’s scenery and props are transcribed in Kirchmeyer, K012, “Summary”. The description of the caricature is our reading of that staging. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka

cues.title: Dance of the Ballerina, cornet and drum
cues.text: The Ballerina enters carrying a toy brass instrument. Her dance opens with solo cornet and military drum, the cornet playing a quick tune over short drum strokes.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, p. 83, rehearsal 69, Dance of the Ballerina, “Cornet in Hand”; the opening is scored for solo cornet and military drum. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Waltz on tunes by Lanner
cues.text: The waltz begins with an accompaniment on solo bassoon, marked grottesco. Cornet and flute take the melody. The tunes are borrowed from Joseph Lanner.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, p. 84, rehearsals 71–72; Lanner borrowings identified by Gerald Larner. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf https://geraldlarner.com/work/stravinsky-petrushka-1911
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Moor joins the Ballerina’s waltz
cues.text: The Ballerina’s waltz is in three beats to the bar. Underneath it, her partner continues his heavy dance in two. Cor anglais and contrabassoon double the lower strings in his tune, and her melody continues above.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, pp. 84–88, from rehearsal 72; Larner describes the Moor joining the waltz in duple time. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf https://geraldlarner.com/work/stravinsky-petrushka-1911
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Petrushka’s entrance, rehearsals 76–78
cues.text: The couple listen. Stopped horns and muted trumpets enter during the waltz, and Petrushka’s cry grows louder among them. He appears, and the quarrel begins.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, pp. 89–91, rehearsals 76–78: the couple listen, Petrushka appears, then the quarrel begins. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: End of the third tableau
cues.text: The Ballerina runs away from the fight. The Moor drives Petrushka out of his room, and the curtain falls. Outside, the fair carries on into the evening.
cues.evidence: Original scenario, end of the third tableau and opening of the fourth, transcribed in Kirchmeyer, K012. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka

transitions.title: Strings subside into Sostenuto
transitions.from: A · Offstage drums and Feroce chords
transitions.to: B · Bassoons, clarinet and bass clarinet
transitions.how: The loud string figures die down into Sostenuto. Bassoons hold a chord and the tuba holds a long low note. Timpani and muted strings set up the repeating accompaniment. Clarinet and bass clarinet then begin the Moor’s tune in octaves.

transitions.title: Drum and cornet alone
transitions.from: B · Bassoons, clarinet and bass clarinet
transitions.how: The low accompaniment stops. At Allegro the military drum enters alone, and the cornet joins it with the Ballerina’s tune. Bassoons, tuba and strings rest for the length of her dance.

transitions.title: Flute flourish, then a waltz
transitions.to: D · Lanner waltzes against duple metre
transitions.how: A brief Appassionato outburst in winds and strings ends with a descending flute flourish and a pause. The bassoon then plays an accompaniment in triple time, marked Lento cantabile and grottesco. Cornet and flute enter with the waltz tune, marked sentimentalmente.

transitions.title: Petrushka’s cry enters in the brass
transitions.from: D · Lanner waltzes against duple metre
transitions.how: At Vivace (rehearsals 76–77), the waltz thins to repeated viola chords and stopped horns. Muted trumpets and cornets play Petrushka’s cry again, with a crescendo from pianissimo. The two dancers stop when they hear him, and then Petrushka bursts into the room.
transitions.evidence: Édition Russe score, p. 89, rehearsals 76–77; the couple’s reaction precedes Petrushka’s appearance. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

source.title: Stravinsky, Petrushka, 1911 orchestration; Édition Russe plate R.M.V. 127, Dover reprint
source.locator: Printed pp. 78–95, rehearsals 62–81. Public-domain score in the US, not the EU. Passage timings are provisional, guided by cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-moor.txt. Both harps share one stage position; active groups vary within the indicated passage.

timeline.note: The introduction combines orchestral gestures with string weight.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 78, rehearsals 62–63; opening changes at 0:12 and 0:26.

timeline.note: A slower, low-centred passage prepares the main melody.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 79, rehearsal 64; low spectral centroids at 0:25–0:40.

timeline.note: Clarinet and bass clarinet double the principal tune in octaves.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 79–80, rehearsal 65; 0:48 boundary followed by a stable pitch profile through 1:35.

timeline.note: The Ballerina’s dance begins with solo cornet and military drum.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 83, rehearsal 69; 3:14 change and brighter but quiet following passage.

timeline.note: The first waltz phrase uses flute, cornet and bassoon.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 84, rehearsal 71; low relative levels and brightness at 3:55–4:05.

timeline.note: The waltz’s upper line is played over a heavier accompaniment in the low register.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 84–88, rehearsals 72–75; internal boundaries at 4:50 and 5:04, followed by a broad increase in level.

timeline.note: Muted brass and stopped horns play at the interruption of the dancing pair.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 89, rehearsal 76; change at 6:24 before increased brightness at 6:30–6:40.

timeline.note: The quarrel begins in bassoon and strings before further winds enter.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 91, rehearsal 78; 6:46 boundary and renewed activity towards the 7:05–7:15 crest. The exact bassoon entrance is not aligned.

fields.label: Work version

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying 1911 composition and original 1912 score are public domain in the United States; the ordinary EU life-plus-70 composition term has not expired.
fields.note: Stravinsky died in 1971, giving an ordinary EU term through 31 December 2041. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance, and it does not grant rights in modern editions, stage designs or choreography. The viewable score is hosted in the US; recording-term eligibility below does not clear the underlying composition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — first lawful publication anywhere before 1963: London CS 6009, commercially published by 1958. Territorial EU sound-recording basis only; US sound-recording status is not established.
fields.note: A contemporary London/Pecar Electronics advertisement in the Grosse Pointe News, 6 November 1958, p. 7, pictures this Petrushka/Ansermet cover with catalogue CS 6009 under recordings NOW AVAILABLE. This directly establishes commercial availability in 1958; Archive’s 1958 carrier date and Decca’s ℗ 1958 attribution corroborate it. The rule concerns first lawful publication anywhere, not first EU publication; the US advertisement is therefore pertinent. A 1958 lawful publication exhausted the former 50-year EU performance/phonogram term by the end of 2008, before the 1 November 2013 protection threshold for the 70-year extension. The exact earliest market/day and any earlier issue are not established or required for this pre-1963 finding. No CC licence, worldwide public-domain claim, or US recording clearance is asserted.

composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: Composer of dance music in which a single displaced accent could unsettle the dancers, and of a psalm setting that scarcely moves.
facts: Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes · Ramuz’s travelling theatre · Balanchine · Auden and Kallman
Ballets, operas, symphonies and sacred music; composing and recording into his eighties
composer.background:
Stravinsky was born in 1882 at Oranienbaum. His father, Fyodor, sang bass at the Mariinsky Theatre in St Petersburg; Igor heard him on stage and began piano lessons at nine. He entered St Petersburg University to study law. There he befriended Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, whose father heard his first pieces in 1902. Rimsky-Korsakov took him on privately, giving regular lessons from 1905 until his death in 1908. The pupil orchestrated pages of Pan Voyevoda, then had to explain why his teacher had scored them differently.

He married his cousin Catherine Nossenko in 1906; by 1914 they had four children. His E♭ Symphony owed much to Glazunov and Tchaikovsky; Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks are short orchestral works. Sergei Diaghilev heard his music in 1909 and gave him some Chopin to orchestrate for Les Sylphides. A full ballet, The Firebird, followed. Stravinsky handed over the score in sections while Michel Fokine worked out the dances. In his 1936 autobiography he recalled that the rehearsals ended with dinner beside Diaghilev and Nijinsky, and good claret.
